lines: Two engineers are arguing over whether their pipeline really deserves that one precise, overused label.
Neither one can actually say which of two specific moments their system protects against.
A live run settles it on the spot, producing a real duplicate from each one in turn.
Here's the right way to state each of these three promises.
Not how many times the system tries to deliver something.
How many times the actual effect of that delivery ends up landing, once everything settles.
Worth reasoning through before the reveal settles it.
A batch goes out, the broker writes it successfully, and then the confirmation back never arrives.
With nothing else turned on, what does the sender actually do next?
answer: It tries again, because it has no way to know the first attempt actually landed.
And without one extra safeguard turned on, that second attempt writes a second, duplicate copy.

lines: Seeing no confirmation, the sender does exactly what it would do after a real failure.
It sends again.
Nothing on the receiving end recognizes this as a repeat, so a second copy lands right next to the first.
Worth reasoning through before the next reveal settles it.
A reader processes one record, writes its effect somewhere, and crashes before saving how far it got.
When a fresh process picks up right after that, what does it actually see?
answer: It resumes from the last position it actually managed to save.
That's still the old one, so the record it already handled gets handled all over again.

lines: On restart, the reader starts exactly where its last saved position says to start.
The record it already finished gets picked up again, from scratch.
Whatever effect that record caused downstream now happens a second time.
Here's the phrase worth being suspicious of: claiming the hard part is solved without ever saying where.
Saying the middle of the pipeline behaves perfectly names no actual boundary.
The moment the final destination isn't built to shrug off a repeat, that same duplicate effect slips right back in, no matter how well everything before it behaved.
Take that same exact crash and run it through each of the three promises in turn.
One of them can let the effect vanish entirely.
Another can let it double. Only the third one holds it at exactly once, every single time, through the very same crash.
Every number in this reel so far came from one real run of this topic's own toy delivery model, happening just now.
Both of the moments it walked through, confirmed directly rather than just described.
And that same three-way comparison, measured instead of assumed.
So: three promises, each one really a statement about how many times an effect lands, not how many times something was attempted.
Two moments where things go wrong, a sender side and a reader side, sharing the exact same shape underneath.
And that one overused label only ever means something once you've named the specific boundary it's supposed to hold at.
